title: Leaders Who Blame and Shame
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece critiques a common but corrosive corrective tactic: publicly calling out a team or individual for dropping the ball as a way to spur better effort. While the essay concedes 'Blame and Shame' can produce a short-term bump in performance, it argues the approach erodes trust over time, making team members withhold bad news and resist future feedback. As an alternative, it recommends leaders work alongside underperforming team members on the task itself, using that shared effort to model standards and rebuild the relationship rather than simply demanding more.
points: 'Blame and Shame' can produce short-term compliance but degrades trust and suppresses bad-news reporting over the long run.
Public accusation lingers with team members far longer than the moment of admonishment itself.
Frequent confrontation over performance builds resistance rather than improvement, per the article's claim.
The recommended alternative is co-executing the task with the underperforming team member rather than simply demanding better results.
Working side-by-side is framed as a trust-building substitute for confrontation, not just a performance fix.
quotes: Far too often, they engage in what is called Blame and Shame.
The Blame and Shame strategy can be highly effective on the short term or in an instance. Over the long term, however, it can erode trust and respect.

This is because accusation and embarrassment linger with team members for much longer than the admonishment. Moreover, team members build up a resistance to being confronted over performance if it happens too frequently.
When reminders and nudges don’t work to push the team and team members toward better execution, the better strategy is for the leader to engage in the task or assignment with them.
Good leaders use blame and shame sparingly, if at all. They work with team members to raise their standards and get the job done on time.
